subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Health Claims and Science
description: A micro-lesson that makes Health Claims and Science usable.

hook.text: Green tea prevents cancer, boosts metabolism, and extends life—at least, that's what the headlines say.

buildup.text: Tea contains catechins, powerful antioxidants. EGCG, the most studied, shows promise in lab settings.

discovery.text: Population studies link regular tea drinking to lower heart disease and stroke risk across multiple countries.

twist.text: Lab results rarely translate to human benefits at normal doses. Most miracle claims are overhyped.

climax.text: The honest conclusion: tea is probably good for you, but it's not medicine. Enjoy it, don't worship it.

punchline.text: Healthy habit? Yes. Miracle cure? Not quite.

quiz.question: What is EGCG?
options: A catechin antioxidant found in green tea

details.summary: Tea has been associated with health benefits for millennia. Modern research confirms it contains potent antioxidants called catechins, particularly EGCG in green tea.
details.whyItMatters: Separating verified science from marketing hype helps consumers make informed choices. Tea has genuine health benefits but is not the cure-all some claim.
takeaways: Tea contains powerful antioxidants called catechins
EGCG in green tea is the most studied beneficial compound
Regular consumption is linked to reduced cardiovascular risk

faq.question: Which type of tea is healthiest?
faq.answer: Green tea and white tea have the highest levels of catechins because they are minimally processed. Matcha delivers even more because the whole leaf is consumed. However, all true teas contain beneficial compounds. The healthiest tea is the one you actually enjoy drinking regularly.

faq.question: Can tea really prevent cancer?
faq.answer: Laboratory studies show tea compounds can inhibit cancer cell growth, but human clinical trials have produced mixed results. Regular tea consumption may reduce risk for certain cancers, but it is not a guaranteed preventive measure.
